Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

any adjective

in questions, conditions and after a negative

also not any, without any, if any, any at all, any you like

classical

Liv. 21.27.5: sine ūllā mōle
Verg. G. 2.420: nōn ūlla est oleīs cultūra

ūllus, ūlla, ūllum

adjective; gen. ūllīus, dat. ūllī · Declension on Wiktionary

any (after a negative, and in questions that expect “no”)

Lewis & Short: ūllus stands in denials where an affirmation has aliquī, as quisquam does for aliquis (see anyone, anything). So after nōn, nec, sine and vix. “Not any” is nūllus (see no).

Other words

  • quī, qua (quae), quod — any (after sī, nisi, num, nē)

    adjective (the indefinite quī) · also used · classical · Cic. Off. 1.7: num quod officium aliud aliō majus sit (Lewis & Short); Caes. BG 1.48: sī quī graviōre vulnere acceptō equō dēciderat (Lewis & Short) · Wiktionary

    After sī, nisi, num and nē the ali- of aliquī drops, as in sī quis, sī quid (see someone, something).

  • quīvīs, quaevīs, quodvīs — any at all, any you like

    adjective and pronoun · also used · classical · Ter. Ad. 254: ab quīvīs homine … beneficium accipere gaudeās (Lewis & Short, Ad. 2.3.1) · Wiktionary

    Any whatever, no matter which; also quīlibet (see anyone, anything, in the sense “no matter who, what”).

Examples

  • Hispānī sine ūllā mōle in utrēs vestīmentīs conjectīs ipsī caetrīs superpositīs incubantēs flūmen trānāvēre

    the Spaniards, without any fuss, put their clothes in leather bags, lay on their shields on top of them and swam the riverLiv. 21.27.5

  • contrā nōn ūlla est oleīs cultūra

    olives, on the other hand, need no tending of any kindVerg. G. 2.420

  • quod amant locum pūrum neque ipsī ūllum, ubi fuērunt, relincunt pūrum

    because they love a clean place, and yet themselves leave no place clean where they have beenVarr. RR 3.10.7

  • ex quō togam virīlem sūmpsit nūllō diē prius ūllam pūblicam prīvātamque rem ēgit quam in Capitōlium īret

    from the day he took the toga of manhood, he did no business of any kind, public or private, before going up to the CapitolLiv. 26.19.5

  • quaeritur, num quod officium aliud aliō majus sit

    the question is whether any duty is greater than anotherCic. Off. 1.7 (Lewis & Short)

See also someone, anything, some, no, anyone.
